title: Wilt thou be made whole (John 5:1–9)
hook: a man ill thirty-eight years is asked if he wants to be healed
tomorrow: I am the bread of life

segments.voice: Yesterday, fields white for harvest and the Samaritans coming up the road. Your line was lift up your eyes.

Near the sheep gate in Jerusalem there's a pool with five porches, covered walkways around the water. The Douay-Rheims calls it Probatica, from the Greek for sheep; most Bibles know it as Bethesda. The porches are full of the blind, the lame, the withered, lying on mats, waiting. People said that now and then the water was stirred, and the first one in would be healed. One man has been lying there thirty-eight years under his illness, John tells us. Today Jesus finds him and asks a question that sounds almost rude.
screen: `A POOL WITH FIVE PORCHES.` → `A CROWD WAITING FOR THE WATER.` → `THIRTY-EIGHT YEARS.`

segments.voice: Jesus knows he has been that way a long time, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wilt thou be made whole?" Do you want to get well? On the surface it's absurd. Of course he does. But listen: he doesn't say yes. "Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pond." Someone always gets there first. It's an explanation, and a lonely one. After thirty-eight years, the story he tells about his life has become: it's never going to be me. Jesus doesn't argue with the story, and he doesn't carry him to the water. He says: "Arise, take up thy bed, and walk." And immediately the man is made whole, picks up his mat, and walks. The question matters because a man ill for thirty-eight years has a whole life built around it: a place to lie, a way of asking, a way of being seen. Being made whole means standing up into a life he doesn't know yet. The Church teaches that God respects our freedom, even in healing; grace is offered, not forced. Two honest notes. Some old manuscripts include a verse about an angel stirring the water; many of the earliest leave it out, and modern Catholic Bibles often put it in a footnote. And the pool is real: near the Church of Saint Anne in Jerusalem, archaeologists found two large pools with a wall between them, which some think explains the five porches.
screen: `WILT THOU BE MADE WHOLE?` · `SIR, I HAVE NO MAN.` · `ARISE, TAKE UP THY BED.` · `A REAL POOL BY SAINT ANNE'S.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you've been stuck a long time, a habit, a hurt, a fear, a relationship gone flat, and hear the question gently: do you want to be made whole? Notice your first answer, a yes or a reason like his, and just hear it without judging. If you pray, give God your honest answer; if not, just let yourself know what it is.
Wilt thou be made whole. Jesus's question to a man ill for thirty-eight years by the pool of Bethesda, before he told him to rise and walk. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: wilt thou be made whole. A gentle question, and then: arise. That's day five hundred two.

chat.says: Why would Jesus ask a man sick for years if he wanted to get well? Isn't that obvious?
options: His life was built around his illness; being made whole meant a new life, offered, not forced.
It was a test of whether he could reach the stirred water before anyone else.
It was simply a polite greeting, the usual way people said hello back then.
chat.meaning: After thirty-eight years, healing would change everything. The Church teaches that God respects our freedom: grace is offered, not forced.

notes: Douay John 5:2 names the pool 'Probatica' and says it is called in Hebrew 'Bethsaida'; most modern Bibles read Bethesda. The script says 'most Bibles know it as Bethesda'. Confirm.
John 5:3b–4 (the angel) is absent from many early manuscripts and footnoted in the NABRE; stated generally. Confirm.
Excavations at St Anne's (two pools with a central dividing wall, possibly the fifth portico): confirm phrasing.
'The Church teaches that God respects our freedom' (softened in review from 'has always taught') — general (cf. CCC 1730–1742); confirm.
Original: ὑγιής and its link to 'hygiene' (via Hygieia): confirm.
